passage:
The group chat lit up every evening at nine, and Aiko loved it. In her bedroom in Osaka she typed jokes about the rival singer's fans, the others sent back laughing faces, and a tight, warm feeling of belonging spread through her chest.
Tonight the target was a girl who had posted a fan drawing. Aiko wrote something cruel about it and got twelve reactions.
Then the girl replied that she was deleting her account, because messages like these had come for three days. Aiko's hands went cold.
Yuki, her classmate, texted her privately: "That was us, wasn't it?"
Aiko stared at the screen for a long time, typed "yes", muted the group and left it. She missed the noise at first, and sat with the quiet.

qa.q: How many reactions did Aiko's cruel message get?
Why did Aiko's hands go cold when the girl replied?
qa.a: She realised her joke had hurt a real person who was now deleting her account, and the warm belonging she had enjoyed turned into guilt.

qa.q: What could Aiko do after leaving the group?
qa.a: She could avoid joining such chats again, look for fan spaces that stay kind, and, if she feels able, apologise to the girl or tell an adult if the abuse goes on.

qa.q: How might the girl who posted the drawing have felt over those three days?
qa.a: She probably felt targeted and unwelcome for something she had made with care, which may be why she chose to delete her account.

grounding: Shows a teen joining rival-fan abuse, enjoying belonging, then seeing the hurt and stepping out.

passage:
Week one. Sachin had joined the fan page for his favourite actor in the summer. Now, before the new film, the page had a "war" with fans of the rival star. Sachin posted a meme calling the rival's fans "brainless." Two hundred laughing reacts. He felt like part of something big.

Week two. The page started targeting individual accounts: people who posted about the rival's film. Someone posted a screenshot of a girl's comment with her photo. "Tag her and roast." Sachin scrolled to see who it was and his stomach turned. It was Jyoti, from his tuition class. Hundreds of comments about her face, her weight.

He didn't comment. But he didn't report it either. At tuition, Jyoti sat alone and wouldn't look up.

Week three. Sachin left the page. He reported the screenshot post. Then, at the end of tuition, he walked up to Jyoti. "I was on that page. I'm sorry. I reported the post." Jyoti stared at him for a long moment. Then she nodded, once.

qa.q: How many laughing reacts did Sachin's meme get?
qa.a: Sachin's meme got two hundred laughing reacts.

qa.q: What was Sachin feeling when he saw Jyoti's photo on the page?
qa.a: Sachin felt sick and guilty, his stomach turning, when he saw a real classmate being targeted.

qa.q: What did Sachin do in week three, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Sachin left the page, reported the post and apologised to Jyoti, which stepped out of the cruelty and took responsibility.

qa.q: What was it like for Jyoti at tuition in week two?
qa.a: Jyoti seemed hurt and humiliated, sitting alone and unable to look up after hundreds of cruel comments.

grounding: It shows a teen who joins fans abusing rival fans online, notices that belonging feels good but hurts real people, and steps out when it turns cruel.

passage:
Amandeep, you think these online fan fights are new? Let your Reena Masi tell you about 1998.

We had a fan club at school for one film hero, and there was another club for his rival. We made posters, wrote slogans on each other's desks. It felt wonderful, like having a family.

Then it turned nasty. There was a girl, Poonam, the only one in our class who liked the rival hero. We started leaving notes in her bag. Mean things about her looks. I wrote one too. Everyone laughed, and I felt so included.

One day I found her crying in the girls' toilet, the note in her hand. My handwriting. I'll never forget her face.

I left the club that week. I went to her and said sorry. She didn't forgive me for a long time, and she didn't have to.

So when your group starts roasting someone, Amandeep, remember: it feels like belonging. But a real person is holding that note.

qa.q: Where did young Reena find Poonam crying?
qa.a: She found her crying in the girls' toilet.

qa.q: What was young Reena feeling when the club laughed at her note?
qa.a: Reena felt included and happy to belong, which made the cruelty feel acceptable at the time.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Reena Masi's story, and why?
qa.a: Finding Poonam crying with Reena's own note was the turning point, because it showed the real hurt behind the group fun and led her to leave and apologise.

qa.q: What was it like for Poonam to be the only fan of the rival hero?
qa.a: Poonam was probably lonely and frightened, targeted by notes about her looks and ending up crying alone.

grounding: It shows an elder recalling joining a fan club's cruelty towards a rival fan, noticing how belonging felt good but hurt a real person, and stepping out.
